one_liner: Header-only, fixed-capacity callable wrapper beating std::function's invocation speed in 5 of 7 shootout categories.
what_it_does: stdext::inplace_function<Signature, Capacity, Alignment> is a type-erased callable wrapper like std::function, but it stores the callable inline in a fixed-size buffer instead of on the heap. It exposes the same copy/move/operator()/operator-bool surface, plus two extra non-type template parameters (Capacity, default 32; Alignment); a callable that doesn't fit is a compile-time static_assert failure, not a runtime allocation. It comes from SG14 (WG21's low-latency/games/embedded study group) and has an associated standards proposal, Docs/Proposals/NonAllocatingStandardFunction.pdf, for a future std::inplace_function.
how_it_is_fast: It avoids the heap allocation std::function performs for non-trivial or captured callables: the object is placement-new'd into an inline aligned_storage buffer sized at compile time, and a small per-type vtable (invoke/copy/relocate/destroy function pointers) replaces the allocator plus type-erasure machinery libstdc++/MSVC use. This removes the allocate/deallocate pair on construction/destruction and an extra pointer indirection to heap-owned state, which is what the CxxFunctionBenchmark invocation timings pick up for stateful callables.
when_to_use: The callable's captured/bound state fits a known small size (tested here at 40 bytes) and that bound can be enforced at compile time.
Hot path repeatedly invokes an already-assigned callable (function pointers, member-fn delegates, small functors) and heap traffic is the std::function cost you're trying to remove.
Embedded, low-latency, or game code where dynamic allocation is undesirable or banned.
You're willing to hand-tune per-callsite capacity/alignment template arguments instead of using one universal type.
MSVC or GCC/Clang toolchain with plain standard C++ (no platform-specific requirements).
when_not_to_use: Callable sizes are unknown or unbounded at the call site: std::function's heap fallback always compiles, inplace_function doesn't.
Capturing/stateless lambdas dominate the workload: in this benchmark inplace_function was slower than std::function for lambda_capture (0.1851s vs 0.1757s) and stateless_lambda (0.1845s vs 0.1799s).
Code crosses shared-library/DLL boundaries: open issue #170 flags ABI concerns for inplace_function used at library edges.
You need an actively maintained dependency: last commit 2022-04-19, repo is abandoned, and 19 issues are open, several unresolved design questions.
You need real concurrency guarantees: open issue #158 notes operator() is const but backed by a mutable, non-atomic buffer, so 'const-callable' isn't a thread-safety guarantee.

integration.dependencies: none (single header; uses <type_traits>, <utility>, <functional> from the standard library)
integration.min_toolchain: C++14 (repo's own alternate build command compiles with -std=c++14; header uses std::exchange and documents an aligned_storage workaround for older GCC/MSVC 32-bit)
integration.platforms: any (portable standard C++, no SIMD/OS-specific code); the benchmark numbers here are MSVC 64-bit only
integration.thread_safety: not documented; open issue #158 disputes whether the const operator() implies thread-safety, since the object's storage is declared mutable
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — explain: same copy/move/call/operator-bool surface as std::function, but the template takes extra Capacity/Alignment parameters, requires the wrapped type to be copy-constructible (static_assert) and to fit the chosen capacity/alignment (static_assert, compile-time failure), and has no allocator fallback for callables that don't fit.

gotchas: Assigning a callable larger than Capacity or overaligned relative to Alignment is a hard compile error, not a runtime allocation; issue #160 'Giant Sized Buffers Required for Compilation' documents this surfacing in practice.

Calling an empty (default-constructed or moved-from) inplace_function throws std::bad_function_call by default via the SG14_INPLACE_FUNCTION_THROW macro, which can be redefined before including the header to opt out of exceptions.
operator() is declared const, but the underlying storage_ member is mutable, so a const inplace_function can still run a mutating call operator (see issue #158).
License lives only in the header's comment block (Boost Software License 1.0); the SG14 repository itself has no license field set on GitHub.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick inplace_function over Delegate (bdiamand/Delegate) when compile-time capacity enforcement and WG21 pedigree (a standards proposal exists to make this std::inplace_function) matter more than raw speed — Delegate wins all 7 categories of the same CxxFunctionBenchmark shootout, where inplace_function only wins 5 of 7. Pick SmallFunction or woid instead for a smaller, single-purpose library without SG14's monorepo and open design questions.
verified_claims_summary: Third-party CxxFunctionBenchmark (jamboree/CxxFunctionBenchmark, various.cpp) times stdext::inplace_function<int(int),40> against std::function<int(int)> on MSVC 64-bit/Visual Studio 15.9.4, Release build: inplace_function is faster in 5 of 7 invocation categories (e.g. 0.2365s vs 0.2640s for function_pointer, 0.1593s vs 0.1906s for compile_time_delegate) but slower for lambda_capture (0.1851s vs 0.1757s) and stateless_lambda (0.1845s vs 0.1799s); no CPU model or exact compiler flags are given beyond 'Release Build'.
status_note: Abandoned since the last commit on 2022-04-19 (a repo-wide date covering all SG14 proposals, not just this header); BSL-1.0 licensed and small enough (one ~200-line header) to vendor regardless, but carries 19 open issues including unresolved questions about exception-free use and shared-library ABI.
